items.title: Touch-screen MacBook Pro will be unveiled on October 28
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly preparing an October 28 launch for a series of iPad and Mac releases, ranging from the OLED touch-screen MacBook Pro to a new iPad mini.

Following its unveiling of the HomeView on October 12, 2026 with briefings and videos rather than an event, Apple is now expected to do the same again. According to Bloomberg, an extensive all-day press briefing is now scheduled for Wednesday, October 28.

Apple is now inviting some media to an all-day product launch experience on Oct. 28 in Los Angeles. This is for the touch-screen MacBooks, iPad mini, M6 Macs.

This second launch has been rumored for some time, and believed to center on the expected OLED touch-screen MacBook Pro. There has also been speculation that it might feature a mixture of Mac and iPad launches.

Specifically, an updated iPad mini with an OLED screen has been predicted. Rumors claim that it will have an 8.4-inch LTPS rear panel with hybrid OLED, but also a 60Hz refresh rate and so no ProMotion.

The new claim that the October 28 unveiling will include M6 Macs, plural, could mean the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 16-inch MacBook Pro, but most likely refers to the iMac. It's now two years since the iMac was updated, and previous reports have claimed that an M6 version would be released before the end of 2026.

It could be quite close to the end of the year, though. If an M6 iMac is launched on October 28, it's unlikely that it will be shipping that day.

Instead, it's much more likely that pre-orders will open in early November, with shipping between the middle and the end of the month. Apple will presumably want the earliest date possible, as an iMac could be a big seller for the holiday season.

The new HomeView could well be the same. That would help Apple's earnings, as this year, it does not have a new base iPhone in its lineup.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro demand takes Apple to a $5 trillion market valuation
items.content_html:
Apple has briefly touched the $5 trillion valuation mark before, but its seemingly unstoppable rise has now taken it back up there again on the back of strong iPhone demand.

Back in October 2025, Apple closed at over $4 trillion for the first time, and then on July 28, 2026, it crossed the $5 trillion mark. It wasn't very long before it dipped back under that to be a paltry $4 trillion and change, but now it's back.

At close of market, Apple's valuation once again passed $342.61, which means it has exceeded $5 trillion. It barely squeaked by, closing at $342.96 or $5.005T.

The valuation appears to be chiefly because of the strong demand for the iPhone 18 Pro in spite of reports suggesting production cuts were a problem. The stock dipped and recovered within the week.

Back in July 2026, Tim Cook cautioned that availability was going to become a problem, but not because of the global chip shortage. "Let me stress this again," Tim Cook said during his last earnings call, "this isn't a partner or supplier issue. This issue is an incredibly strong demand."

At time of writing, online orders for the iPhone 18 Pro Max are showing a shipping date of around three weeks. But it's taken longer to get to that point than usual, and that suggests that Apple has been able to meet demand more than expected.

The issues of the global chip shortage are continuing, though, and this holiday season is usually Apple's biggest. That may change, at least slightly, as the iPhone 18 and possibly iPhone 18e or iPhone Air 2 launches have been pushed back to spring 2027.

What's likely to happen is that Apple will see demand shift from the Pro models to the base one exactly as it makes that launch. So there's probably going to be a consistency of revenue-generating iPhone launches.

All of which ignores how well Services have performed for the company. It's also possible that the much-awaited improvements to Siri AI are going to drive sales and keep that valuation rising.

items.title: That five-year-old Apple TV 4K is getting Siri AI
items.content_html:
Apple's new Siri AI is coming to Apple TV 4K models dating back to 2021, giving existing owners the upgraded assistant without a $299 hardware purchase.

The new Siri AI beta will work on Apple TV 4K models dating back to the second generation, so owners won't need to buy the latest hardware to use the upgraded assistant.

The feature brings a more conversational version of Siri to the television, with natural-language searches, follow-up questions, and personalized recommendations. It also introduces a full-screen interface for exploring movies and TV shows.

Users can ask Siri which Apple TV shows won Emmy Awards, request recommendations, or ask questions about something they're watching. Responses appear in a compact overlay during playback, allowing viewers to continue watching without interrupting the screen.

Siri AI will be available in beta with tvOS 27.2 on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later). The feature requires the home's owner to have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software, with Siri AI enabled in a supported language.

With a compatible device paired, Siri can also access personal context to handle requests such as playing a show recommended by someone in a message.

At launch, Siri AI will support English in eight countries, including the United States, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the United Kingdom.

The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K adds three far-field microphones for hands-free Siri commands, even while audio is playing. Older Apple TV 4K models also support Siri AI, but lack the new model's built-in microphones.

items.title: Where Apple focused engineering so the iPhone Duo could have desktop-like performance
items.content_html:
To make the iPhone Duo as thin as it is, Apple needed to make a lot of design choices to fend off heat. Here's what they did, how they did it, and where in the device the innovations live.

Folding devices like the iPhone Duo often raise engineering challenges due to their unique design. However, solving problems like making as thin a smartphone as possible can lead to the creation of others, such as keeping it cool.

In an interview with PCMag, Apple's VP of silicon engineering Dan Murray and senior manager of thermal product design Banafsheh Barabadi discussed how Apple fixed heat issues in the iPhone Duo.

The discussion first covered the "M-Class-inspired packaging design" of the A20 Pro, referring to a change from the package-on-package (POP) process Apple previously used. Rather than a vertical stack for the system-on-chip (SOC) and the memory, Apple moved the DRAM module next to the processor.

The "M-Class" stems from the idea that a notebook like a MacBook Pro has a lot more internal space to play with than a smartphone. The memory can easily be placed separately from the processor, rather than requiring it to be stacked to save space.

The use of a wafer-level multichip module (WMCM) packaging technique helped spread out the heat instead of confining it to one place. The location also meant that the memory still had fast communications with the chip itself.

While Apple has used vapor chambers in the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, Apple redesigned the idea for the A20 Pro used in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The chassis were also redesigned to work better with the thermal technique.

There are four pillars to heat management, with the first being direct silicon access. The shifting of the DRAM from the vertical stack helped this, since heat from the silicon has a more direct path to the vapor chamber.

"Metal over foam" is the second pillar, creating a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the vapor chamber and chip. "It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right," the engineers explained.

The technique was first spotted during a teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, described at the time as "thermal chainmail" inside a pad.

The third is the vapor chamber, which now as three times the surface area as the previous version, along with more de-ionized water. The chamber also serves as the "central structural plane for the device," said Barabadi, with the battery and logic board mounted directly to it.

Lastly, the fourth is a new layer on the back of the foldable display to keep it sturdy. It's described as a "nanotube copper display metal plate material" that provides mechanical strength for the display.

The copper plate also has a high level of thermal conductivity, combined with a high-conductivity graphite layer. The result is that heat is spread more evenly across the display, reducing hotspots.

"When we combine these four pillars together, it meaningfully improves the thermal performance across every metric," said Barabadi.

The thermal antics aren't just limited to the main body of the iPhone Duo. The all-important hinge does its part too.

Since the iPhone Duo has two halves, connected by a hinge, the two thin halves become one much thicker device when closed. For heat management, this is a problem, because the vapor chamber in the iPhone Duo floats in the middle.

To thermally connect the two halves of the chamber, there's a flexible graphite pipe going through the hinge. This transfers heat between the two sides, balancing the temperature throughout the devices.

It also considerably increased the surface area used for heat dissipation.

To Apple, the part needed to be worked on by both the thermal and mechanical teams. All due to being a flexible material that needed to survive thousands of hinge activations throughout the iPhone Duo's lifespan.

items.title: Just about all of 'No Man's Sky' is coming to iPhone and iPad
items.content_html:
Hello Games is bringing "No Man's Sky" to iOS and iPadOS, with preorders for the mobile version starting ahead of its October 28 release date.

"No Man's Sky" is a game that has been around since August 2016, and only became available on Mac as recently as June 2023. Now, over a decade after the initial release, "No Man's Sky" is finally landing on iPhone and iPad.

The sci-fi adventure game is set in a procedurally-generated universe, filled with countless solar systems, planets, and space stations. Starting on the outer rim, players can explore unique planets, build bases, and upgrade their ships as they try to reach the center of the universe.

While it's finally traversing the software landscape to iOS and iPadOS, the release isn't a cut-down version designed for mobile users. Instead, it's the same full universe that players on other platforms already enjoy.

That includes recent updates such as COSMOS, and the 2025 Voyagers update that introduced customizable big-rig starships.

No Man's Sky on an iPad, with interface - Image Credit: Hello Games

However, there are some small concessions, in line with the Nintendo Switch version of the game, following player feedback. There wasn't multiplayer or "settlements" on Day 1, which will be the same on iOS from launch.

It also introduces a new set of touch controls to work with the mobile displays. Players can still elect to play with controllers, mouse and keyboard on an iPad, and casting to a television for big-screen gaming.

As an ambitious game, it does take a hefty amount of storage space, but not as much as you'd think. The developers say that installation is less than 5 gigabytes, despite the sheer scale of the in-game universe.

While it is a ten-year-old game, there were inklings of a move to iPhone and iPad a few years ago.

The WWDC 2022 launch of the Metal 3 API and the MetalFX framework was accompanied by discussion of how it would be used to improve the performance of "No Man's Sky" on Mac. MetalFX is used to manage upscaling, as well as drawing extra frames to improve frame rates.

In a June 2023 interview with AppleInsider for the Mac version's launch, Hello Games CEO Sean Murray talked about how Mac and iOS was something the studio always considers. The move to Metal had taken almost two years at that point, with Apple assisting one year into the effort.

Murray was enthusiastic about the App Store and its reach to new users who may not have heard of his company's games.

However, developing for Mac and iPad are very different tasks. "Suddenly you have to consider a new user interface, battery life, things like that," Murry said, adding that you have to consider how that audience "like to play their games."

At the time, he didn't directly say a mobile edition of "No Man's Sky" was on the way, but hinted at it.

Moving to Vulkan enabled Hello Games to work with Metal, and likewise the move to VR opened up the possibility of developing for the Nintendo Switch and mobile hardware. Murray ended the thought by saying he was excited to see where Metal might lead to, and that it was "just our next step in a longer journey."

The game is available to preorder from the App Store on Monday, October 12 as part of Apple's App Store Indie Games Week. The full release is on October 28, with a free-to-try element at launch.

Unlocking the full game will cost $19.99.

items.title: Apple's $1,499 iPhone Duo repair cost is a strong argument for AppleCare
items.content_html:
After viewing the repair costs on Apple's first foldable, we've got a bit of advice for you: go ahead and add AppleCare to your cart right now.

Apple has released the uninsured repair costs for the iPhone Duo, and they aren't for the faint of heart. Depending on what damage your phone takes, you could pay 75% of the retail value to get it fixed.

Here's what it costs to repair an iPhone Duo, assuming you don't have insurance through your carrier or AppleCare.

The "other damage" category, which typically denotes damage that can't be replaced with a simple component swap, costs nearly $1,500. That's 75% of the $1,999 price tag, assuming you purchased a base-model iPhone Duo.

If you have AppleCare, the prices are significantly lower. Here's what you can expect to pay.

For other damage, AppleCare drops the cost by $1,400, which is roughly 93% cheaper. If nothing else, it's a poignant reminder that investing in a good insurance plan, like AppleCare, can save you a lot of money.

items.title: Apple HomeView hands on: So many questions, but I like it
items.content_html:
At Apple's NYC experience, I got an early look at HomeView, its new smart home display. I still have unanswered questions but my early take is that I like it. A lot.

Most of you have seen the general rundown on the hardware. It's a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, perched atop a speaker base or mounted to a wall that you can control with your voice or touch.

It has Siri AI built-in to operate your smart home, answer questions, find your lost Apple TV 4K Siri Remote, or otherwise control it. There's a built-in camera that can recognize up to six distinct users to load personal information, such as message history or calendars.

The device ships with a series of Apple apps such as Calendar, Safari, Music, and more. Additional apps are supported via your iPhone, like Apple TV.

My first impression was how much I loved the look of it. It's small. Cute even.

HomeView can get very dark, making it great for sitting next to your bed

The display feels just the right size to easily fit onto a night stand, desk, or kitchen counter without being too big. It's a bright display, too, looking crisp and sharp from anywhere, even in the well-lit demo areas.

I love the wealth of faces, as Apple calls them, that it designed for the HomeView. Some of these are entirely new, while others are borrowed from the Apple TV and Apple Watch.

The Flow face reacts to your movements

The Flow face on Apple Watch reacts to your wrist movements, while on the HomeView, it reacts to your movements in the room. One face looks like a sundial, fading the numerals in and out of view over time.

HomeView showing the Snoopy face that reacts to time, the calendar, and the weather.

I've always been a fan of the Snoopy face, and even if I want to put the data-heavy modular face in the kitchen, I fret my children are going to be insistent here. The Snoopy one still animates and takes cues from the calendar and weather, pulling out an umbrella when it's raining.

Not to dwell too much on the idle faces here, but I think the Photos face is also another winner. You can use a shared photo album for this, so if another family member outside the house has a HomeView, it's effortless to contribute new photos to their device.

HomeView sitting on a kitchen counter

I know multiple people who use digital photo frames for this exact reason and Apple easily created a more seamless version that also has a bunch of other features.

These faces all looked very polished and useful. It's going to be hard to decide whether to go with usable controls or gorgeous clock faces.

As I went through the demo home, there were a lot of those little "oh, I love that!" moments the more I used HomeView.

Using HandOff to send over a Recipe in Safari to HomeView

Using HandOff to transfer a recipe into a helpful cooking view is genuinely useful and you can use Siri to move step to step hands-free. It also doesn't require any app or special Apple News link — just a recipe in Safari that can be pinned for future use.

Mirror mode on HomeView with an edge ring light

The mirror was also quite clever. When you get ready for the day, you can open the mirror app to see yourself. HomeView has a closeup view where you can clearly see your face, or you can zoom out for a full-body look.

If it's dark, you can turn on the edge ring light. A similar lighting feature is also available on the Mac.

Beyond the basic uses of the HomeView, what I was here for was the smart home aspect. I desperately want an always-on smart display to control my Apple Home devices and thus far, that functionality has been limited to almost every other ecosystem.

Live camera feed on HomeView

You can do this with an iPad, but it's not the same. There's no multi-user support, ideal dashboard view, perfect mounting option, and I'd also miss intercom and hub functionality.

I specifically wanted a streamlined device that was designed from the beginning to be a smart display, and not a tablet. That's what we got with HomeView.

Someone ringing the doorbell which then shows on HomeView

The camera feed face is perfect to see real-time live camera streams from your home and the modular face lets you choose exactly what accessories you want to prioritize as always available.

Apple has all-new animations and styles for each of the interactions, like controlling the thermostat or lights. They were designed for this screen size and will be easy for anyone to understand and use.

I think one of the most popular uses for HomeView will be replacing your in-wall light switches. This is possible with the AC hardwire mount and something a lot of savvy users will be able to do themselves.

Especially wall mounted, the HomeView is a great place to put your smart home controls

You tie off your lights to be always-on and swap the "dumb" bulb for a smart bulb and you're good to go. I think that's exactly what I'd like to do.

For as bullish as I am on HomeView, I do think there is a lot to come. This, in many ways, feels like Apple's early version of the Apple Watch.

I think having some system-wide gesture would prove useful, instead of tucked away as an accessibility setting. I'd love a gesture that, similar to the double-tap on Apple Watch, could pause a track, move to the next step in a recipe, or end a FaceTime call.

Various apps available on HomeView

It's also not unjustified to ask for more app integrations. I understand Apple's preferred method of interaction is largely voice with simple tasks, but that shouldn't entirely limit HomeView to this awkward CarPlay scenario that only will allow audio and video apps.

We'll have to wait closer to launch, but I'm curious about how widgets will work. The demo units only had Apple's stock apps installed so there wasn't an opportunity to try any CarPlay streaming apps or widgets.

It would be great to have the Matic robovac app on there, which works with Apple Home, but has further cleaning customization within its own app. In the Matic app, I can change the room cleaning order or direct it to a spill.

Recipe apps like Crouton, NYT Cooking, or Paprika seem to be natural fits too. Apple's recipe implementation looks great, but the only recipes you can load are via Safari.

The guided recipe experience on HomeView

I do think that much of this will come down the line, but it does highlight some of the holes in the initial implementation. The good news is the hardware is there and looks gorgeous.

Hopefully we see next steps at WWDC in June. Fingers crossed for a proper pipeline for more third-party integrations.

Right now, I plan on buying at least three HomeViews for my home. Originally, I thought I'd only end up with one in the kitchen.

I want one bedside, which is possible, in part, because of the special low-light mode that lets the display get super dim. This would be a great dashboard to control all the individual smart lights in our room, while also being able to see any security cameras.

We already were planning on putting a HomePod mini in the room. For $150 more, we can get a HomeView with far more utility.

Of course there will be a kitchen one for family use. I'm sure it will be used constantly for cooking, watching YouTube, checking the shared family calendar, or FaceTime calls.

My studio absolutely needs one. I could tie this into all my different scenes for working, filming, or podcasting, plus it would be physical controls for my smart shades.

As HomeView evolves, and we even see more third-party customizations and accessories, this could go further. I'm particularly interested if anyone makes an articulating arm that would allow one to be mounted on my desk.

It's a new device category and admittedly somewhat limited out of the box, but I think the potential is there and I'm very excited to finally start using it. After more than five years of rumors, HomeView is finally here.

items.title: OpenAI cries foul, says Apple stole secrets from it in 2026
items.content_html:
In a new filing, OpenAI claims that it too was victimized by confidential information theft, and implies that Apple's HomeView was somehow influenced by that theft.

Without much detail, OpenAI says that during the forensic investigation that is required by Apple's trade secret theft lawsuit, it discovered trade theft by Apple. In a filing on Wednesday, the company vaguely says that the thief joined OpenAI from Apple, worked at OpenAI for six months, then returned to Apple.

When the alleged thief returned to Apple, they brought with them details of one OpenAI hardware device stashed away in personal accounts. Furthermore, the documents include specific images, engineering info, supplier information, manufacturing data, and standards for cosmetic finishes and sealants.

In short, OpenAI is accusing this employee, who returned to work at Apple in June 2026, of the same thing that Apple alleges. And, in the filing, OpenAI is drawing a spurious and strange parallel to the HomeView, which has been in development for at least three years that we are aware of.

"That presentation appears to have happened months ago," The filing says. "Armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products."

OpenAI claims that the employee made presentations about product plans to Apple's vice president of operations in Asia. The company also says that it has raised this issue with Apple.

Apple reportedly never responded. However, it has denied that the theft or briefing happened, and says there is no evidence surrounding the incident that the company holds.

In a statement to Reuters on Wednesday, Apple says that it has "policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information" from OpenAI, or any other company.

We could not identify the alleged thief. The filing does not say who it is, which in itself is unusual.

Apple alleges that its former employees, Tang Yew Tan and Chang Liu, stole the company's trade secrets through iCloud exploits. They then used that information to benefit OpenAI in an attempt to benefit OpenAI.

According to Apple, the two stole information by continuing to use work-issued devices and services after leaving the company. The two allegedly also abused bugs, emailed themselves supplier information, and instructed Apple employees interviewing with OpenAI to bring unreleased Apple hardware with them.

As a result, Apple filed a lawsuit against its former employees and against OpenAI in July 2026.

Naturally, OpenAI denied the accusations, and said that they had procedures to prevent this kind of thing, and to stop leaks like they are alleging as well.

There has been a considerable amount of legal drama in the last five months, and there will be much more going forward up to and including the trial, which has not been scheduled yet. However, on Tuesday, Judge Edward Davila partly granted Apple's requests for relevant OpenAI information about the employees in question.

items.title: Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Gen 3: What four years of tech advancement gets you
items.content_html:
The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is here, complete with Siri AI enhancements and Find My on the Siri Remote. Here's how much difference four years makes over the previous model.

Before the October 13 update, Apple's last change to the Apple TV 4K took place in October 2022. Back then, the big news was a storage upgrade.

Four years later, and the fourth-generation model is a spec-bump update that does more than just storage. It's part of a big smart home push by Apple, with changes ranging from improvements to how you use Siri to how it handles surround sound audio.

We don't usually expect many changes in the Apple TV 4K, with it usually falling victim to the spec-bump update cycle. With such a long gap between updates, it was certain that Apple would make some worthwhile changes beyond a chip update.

Thankfully, that happened.

What follows is a comparison between the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and the previous third-generation Apple TV 4K.

The 2022 Apple TV 4K was a rounded square, resembling a rectangular hockey puck near your TV. As usual for Apple's spec-bump updates, the appearance hasn't changed at all.

That includes the dimensions. The old model was 3.66 inches square and 1.2 inches tall. The new one is effectively identical.

Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Apple TV 4K Gen 3: The design hasn't really changed externally.

There is a bit more weight to the new model, however, at 7.6 ounces, it's a 0.3-ounce weight gain over the 7.3-ounce predecessor.

That said, for a device destined to sit in the living room and not move, that's not significant.

A staple of the spec-bump update is a change of chip, and there's certainly one here. The old model used an A15 Bionic chip, first introduced in the iPhone 13 line.

The new edition switches it up to the A19, last launched in the iPhone 17. Apple claims that the chip, complete with Secure Enclave, is approximately 50% better in CPU performance and up to twice as fast in GPU performance over the A15 Bionic.

If we look at the comparative smartphones in Geekbench, we can see this difference a bit clearer.

Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Apple TV 4K Gen 3: The new model will be better for gaming.

The single-core results for the iPhone 13's A15 Bionic put it at 1,955, versus 2,998 for the iPhone 17's A19. Likewise, the 4,965 multi-core score of the A15 Bionic is far behind the 8,287 of the A19.

The Metal benchmark, used for GPU performance, is also quite different. At 35,327, the iPhone 17's Metal score is more than double that of the 14,574 seen in the iPhone 13.

While these are iPhone results for the relative chips, it does demonstrate that the Apple TV 4K counterparts have a similar performance disparity. Gaming will inevitably be better on the newer model.

The real benefit of the A19 chip isn't really performance, but Siri AI support. Apple's big push forward on AI has happened everywhere else in the ecosystem, with home devices lagging behind until now.

Sure, old Siri on the third-gen Apple TV answered queries, but never really did so that well. That's not a problem anymore.

The new Apple TV 4K now takes advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, which means it has all of the bells and whistles of the iPhone version. That includes things like a wider knowledge graph of the world and contextual awareness.

Not only can you ask things like which Apple TV shows won awards recently, but you'll see their posters and can ask follow-up queries too. There are also Amazon X-ray-style queries available too, such as "Where was this show filmed?"

Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Apple TV 4K Gen 3: Siri AI in action

And then there's personal context, which means it can take advantage of data points it knows about you and your data from other Apple devices that Siri AI has analyzed. There stands a good chance that you'll get a decent answer to questions like "What was that show Aunt Mildred talked about last week?" and then end up watching the result.

Connected to this is a bit of a hardware change for the Apple TV. While previously you had to talk through the remote control, that's entirely optional now.

A trio of far-field microphones with echo cancellation are now listening to the room, just like a HomePod or HomePod mini. You can now utter "Hey Siri" without gripping the control to start a query through your Apple TV.

To be frank, this could be great for people who don't already own a HomePod. It's a similar feature, but driven through your television.

When it comes to viewing content through the Apple TV 4K, there's not really much difference from the previous version, at least visually.

There's support for 4K 60FPS HDR10+ content on both models, as well as Dolby Vision and HLG support. HDMI Quick Media Switching (QMS) is still there, using the HDMI 2.1 port.

This time around, Apple does include a dedicated AV1 decoder, built into the A19, which will help with viewing some content online.

The list of supported audio formats is also unchanged, with both capable of handling AAC, MP3, Apple Lossless, FLAC, AIFF, WAV, Dolby Digital 5.1, Dolby Digital Plys 7.1 Surround Sound, and Dolby Atmos.

Photo support is also there, with HEIF, JPEG, GIF, and TIFF usable on both generations.

The big viewing party trick for 2026 is the new Surround Sound feature when used with four HomePod speakers. Placed around the corners of the room, the HomePod and HomePod mini pairs can work together, automatically calibrating the audio for a cinematic experience.

This only works with the second-generation HomePod and the new HomePod mini 2.

Yes, you could output audio to a pair of HomePods using AirPlay before, but certainly not in an automatically configured surround setup like this.

The third-gen Apple TV 4K was sold in two configurations. One was a Wi-Fi-only model with 64GB of storage, while the other added in gigabit Ethernet and bumped storage to 128GB.

For the fourth-gen model, Apple's decided to stick with the Ethernet-enabled variant and its 128GB capacity. You can't get a Wi-Fi-only model anymore.

Connectivity has improved a bit over the years, though you're still going to be plugging into an HDMI 2.1 port.

Wi-Fi has grown from Wi-Fi 6 to Wi-Fi 7, with Ethernet still gigabit, though there's no real need to go higher right now.

Bluetooth is also up, going from 5.0 in the Gen 3 to Bluetooth 6 in Gen 4. An IR receiver and Thread support persist through both models.

The Siri Remote in the third-gen model was pretty good, with the updated design being a little bigger than its predecessor. It also had a silver aluminum finish, and finally shifted from Lightning in favor of USB-C for charging.

There are still some subtle changes in the new Siri Remote for the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, despite it looking pretty identical to the previous model.

First, while there's still an IR transmitter and USB-C, the Bluetooth connectivity has been upgraded. It's gone from 5.0 to 6, like the main box.

Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Apple TV 4K Gen 3: Find My will help you find the new Siri Remote.

The other is that it now has Find My support with Precision Finding and an added speaker. No longer will TV viewers be frustrated by losing the remote, as they can now know which direction in the room they need to look by checking their iPhone and listening for the chirp.

The third-gen Apple TV 4K launched back in 2022 with two prices. The Wi-Fi-only 64GB model cost just $129 at launch, with the 128GB Ethernet model at $149.

However, in June, the prices were bumped up to $199 and $249, respectively, thanks to the ongoing memory crisis.

The new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is being sold in one single configuration, priced at $299.

The new Apple TV 4K is in a weird position. There's a lot of good to it, but also one pretty painful element.

As a spec-bump update after a four-year wait, it has what we expect. Better performance, a lot of Siri improvements, and neat tricks like the HomePod surround sound feature.

The big thing about it is Siri AI, or more those external microphones that weren't on the previous model. With the new version, it's almost justifiable not to acquire a HomePod or HomePod mini to go with it if you want the better Siri functionality alone.

Of course, there's the potential to shell out nigh $600 for four HomePod mini 2 units to get the surround sound going.

The only real problem is the price, which is unquestionably an issue.

Apple TV 4K Gen 4 vs Apple TV 4K Gen 3: The new model is better, but also fairly expensive.

The tech industry as a whole suffers from the same problem. The tougher-to-stomach part is that it's $50 more than the previous model's equivalent, which itself was $100 more than its initial launch cost.

It's hard not to feel for those who bought the third-gen model in the last few months of sale, who may be kicking themselves. If they had waited and spent $50 more, they'd have a newer and more future-proofed set-top box.

As it stands, it's very hard to justify telling anyone to upgrade their Apple TV 4K from the third generation to the fourth. It's even hard to say that about the second-generation users, too.

If the price were closer to $200, it'd be easier to talk about that.

The Apple TV 4K 4th Generation retails for $299, with Apple Premier Partner Expercom expected to carry the new set-top box. Easily compare availability and offers in our Apple TV 4K Price Guide.

Adorama has limited Apple TV 4K 3rd Generation inventory available, while eBay has a variety of pre-owned options for sale.

items.title: Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote comes with an unexpected catch
items.content_html:
Apple's new Siri Remote adds Precision Finding, but the feature won't work with iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models, as Apple is using a new Bluetooth-based technology.

Introduced alongside the fourth-generation Apple TV, the updated remote adds more precise location guidance through Find My and a built-in tone inducer that can play a sound when the remote goes missing.

However, Apple's compatibility requirements exclude several relatively recent iPhones, including models that already support advanced location tracking with other Apple accessories.

According to Apple's footnotes, Precision Finding requires an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or iPhone 17 or later, excluding the iPhone 17e. Compatible iPhones must run the latest version of iOS, and availability varies by region.

The restriction is particularly notable because the iPhone 15 lineup and most iPhone 16 models already feature Apple's second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Those iPhones support expanded Precision Finding with the AirTag 2, but they can't use the new Siri Remote's Precision Finding feature.

The reason is that Apple isn't using Ultra Wideband as with AirTag and AirPods. Instead, it's using a new feature recently added to the Bluetooth spec.

In Bluetooth 6, there is a new part of the spec called Channel Sounding, which is likely what Apple is utilizing. Channel Sounding has centimeter-level precision combining Phase-Based Ranging (PBR) and Round-Trip Timing (RTT).

PBR measures the distance in radio signal phases across multiple frequencies and RTT times how long the signals take to go between devices. Together, they mimic UWB functionality at a lower cost as it doesn't require dedicated hardware.

Owners of older iPhones aren't entirely out of options. Since iOS 17, Apple's existing remote finder has helped users locate second-generation and newer Siri Remotes using proximity indicators that show whether they're getting closer to or farther from the device.

Precision Finding provides more detailed location guidance, while the ability to play a sound is exclusive to the fourth-generation Siri Remote. The new Siri Remote is compatible with Apple TV HD and every Apple TV 4K generation, and Apple will sell it separately.

Owners of older Apple TV hardware can therefore upgrade their remote without purchasing the new $299 Apple TV 4K. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is available for preorder starting October 13, with availability beginning November 13.

items.title: New in iOS 27.2 beta 4: Apple Health, Apple Music changes
items.content_html:
While iOS 27.2 beta 4 brought a new look for Apple Music and a reference to a new HomePod setting, it also curiously removed an upcoming Apple Health upgrade. Here's what you need to know.

On Tuesday, shortly after unveiling its HomeView and other smart home products, Apple deployed the fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2. The beta software update bears the build number 24B5110a, up from 24B5099f.

In a particularly noticeable visual change, iOS 27.2 beta 4 removes all color from the Apple Music icon. Now, it's just a black musical note on a white background, or inverted in dark mode, rather than the white and red look the icon has used since iOS 14.

Though it might seem like an unusual stylistic change for Apple to make, it's not the first time the company has altered the color scheme of the Apple Music icon. Before the now-replaced orange color, the Apple Music icon on iOS 8.4 through iOS 13 had a multi-colored note against a white background.

It remains to be seen whether the new black-and-white Apple Music icon will make it to the release version of iOS 27.2, especially as Apple may have delayed another feature. The fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2 outright lacks the redesigned Apple Health app seen in previous beta builds.

The app itself features new AI-powered summaries and suggestions, along with layout changes, among other things. It's expected to arrive with iOS 27.2, though Tuesday's developer beta suggests Apple might have other plans regarding when to release it.

In place of the revamped Apple Health app is a message saying the overhaul is "coming later this year." Data on devices running the latest iOS 27.2 beta remains viewable in the Settings app, though.

Additionally, iOS 27.2 beta 4 has a new setting for HomePods. The new slider is labeled Lock Controls. "When Lock Controls is enabled, touch interactions for touch, touch and hold, and volume are disabled," reads the description.

Overall, the fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2 is a relatively minor update, offering virtually nothing beyond the black-and-white Apple Music icon. Depending on what Apple does with its redesigned Health app, the iOS 27.2 update could prove to be less impressive than initially expected.

items.title: There are better-sounding and cheaper options than four HomePods for surround sound
items.content_html:
Apple's four-HomePod surround sound setup costs at a minimum $900 with a new Apple TV 4K. These five alternatives deliver dedicated wireless rear speakers and more features for considerably less money.

Apple introduced four-speaker HomePod surround sound alongside the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K on October 13. The feature allows compatible HomePods to operate as matching front and rear pairs, with Apple TV automatically calibrating audio timing and levels based on speaker placement.

However, as we reported, the feature requires the new $299 Apple TV 4K and four compatible HomePods. Only second-generation HomePods and HomePod mini 2 models are supported, and the front and rear pairs must match.

Two full-size HomePods cost $698, while two HomePod mini 2 speakers add another $298. Combined with the required Apple TV 4K, the complete system costs $1,295 before taxes. Four HomePod minis bring the total down to $895, while four full-size HomePods push the cost to $1,695.

That's why we're setting an $800 ceiling for competing surround sound systems. Adding the $299 Apple TV 4K keeps the total below $1,100, saving at least $196 compared with Apple's mixed HomePod configuration.

Each of the following systems includes dedicated rear speakers, and four support Apple AirPlay for wireless music streaming. They connect to a television through HDMI ARC/eARC or optical audio rather than relying on Apple's proprietary HomePod surround sound arrangement.

The LG S80TR provides a complete 5.1.3-channel surround sound system with a soundbar, two wireless rear speakers, and a dedicated subwoofer. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X, with three upward-firing speakers designed to reproduce overhead audio effects.

AirPlay 2 support allows music streaming from an iPhone, iPad, or Mac. The soundbar also includes HDMI eARC, LG's AI Room Calibration, and WOW Orchestra, which can combine the soundbar's output with compatible LG televisions.

The rear speakers connect wirelessly to the soundbar and don't require a separate receiver, although each needs a power outlet. That makes the system relatively straightforward to install without running speaker cables across the room.

The LG S80TR is available for $599.99, bringing the total to $898.99 with the new Apple TV 4K.

The JBL Bar 700MK2 takes a different approach to wireless surround sound with two detachable, battery-powered rear speakers. The 7.1-channel system also includes a 10-inch wireless subwoofer and a soundbar with 780 watts of maximum system output.

Users can detach the rear speakers from the ends of the soundbar and position them behind the seating area. The speakers provide up to 10 hours of playback before being returned to the soundbar for charging, eliminating the need for power outlets behind the couch.

JBL includes Dolby Atmos, DTS Virtual:X, AirPlay 2, and HDMI eARC with 4K Dolby Vision passthrough. Its MultiBeam 3.0 technology and automatic sound calibration help create a wider soundstage, while PureVoice 2.0 is designed to improve dialogue clarity.

The JBL Bar 700MK2 is currently on sale for $549.95, down from $899.95. Including the Apple TV 4K, the complete setup costs $848.95.

The LG S90TR increases the speaker configuration to 7.1.3 channels, making it one of the more extensive surround sound systems in this price range. It includes a wireless subwoofer, two wireless rear speakers, and three upward-firing channels for Dolby Atmos audio.

Like the S80TR, it supports AirPlay 2, DTS:X, HDMI eARC, and LG's WOW Orchestra technology. The additional surround channels and 13-speaker configuration provide more dedicated audio sources than the less expensive LG system.

Room Calibration Pro uses the soundbar's built-in microphone to measure the listening environment and adjust playback. The rear speakers connect wirelessly and only require electrical outlets, with no separate receiver needed.

The LG S90TR costs $799.99, bringing the combined price with Apple TV 4K to $1,098.99.

The Sonos Surround Set with Ray combines a compact soundbar with two Era 100 speakers for dedicated rear-channel surround sound. It's designed for smaller rooms and buyers who prefer an expandable audio system rather than a complete home theater package.

The Ray supports AirPlay 2, while the Era 100 speakers serve as wireless surrounds when paired with the soundbar. Sonos also offers multiroom playback, Trueplay tuning on supported devices, and the ability to expand the system with additional compatible hardware.

There are some important compromises. The package doesn't include a subwoofer, and the Ray uses an optical audio connection instead of HDMI eARC. It supports Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound but doesn't support Dolby Atmos.

The Sonos Surround Set costs $622, or $921 when combined with the new Apple TV 4K.

Amazon's Fire TV Soundbar Plus with subwoofer and surround speakers delivers a complete 5.1-channel system for less than $500. The package includes a 37-inch soundbar, a wireless subwoofer, and two wireless rear speakers.

It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X, with a dedicated center channel for dialogue and separate listening modes for movies, music, sports, and nighttime viewing. The subwoofer and rear speakers connect wirelessly to the soundbar, although each requires a power outlet.

Despite its Fire TV branding, the soundbar doesn't require an Amazon streaming device. It connects to compatible televisions through HDMI ARC/eARC or optical audio, allowing it to reproduce sound from an Apple TV connected to the television.

However, the Fire TV Soundbar Plus doesn't offer AirPlay support. Bluetooth streaming is available for music playback, but users won't get the same AirPlay integration offered by the other systems in this roundup.

The Amazon bundle costs $489.99, bringing the total to $788.99 with the new Apple TV 4K.

All five alternatives provide physical rear speakers, although the number of channels, height effects, and subwoofer capabilities vary considerably. AirPlay support lets users stream music wirelessly from Apple devices, but surround sound from Apple TV travels through HDMI or optical audio connections to these systems.

Apple's HomePods offer advantages beyond home theater playback, including independent Siri not tethered by an Apple TV, Apple Home integration, and wireless audio managed directly by Apple TV. However, buyers primarily interested in surround sound have several less expensive options that don't require purchasing four Apple speakers, not reliant on ARC working right for other HDMI connections, and more compatible with other gear.

items.title: Two HomeView home hub models evolve Apple's home strategy at $299 each
items.content_html:
Years of rumors have finally culminated in the 7-inch square HomeView. It's the smart home dashboard you've been waiting for, that ties into the Apple ecosystem.

After a limited first attempt at AI and a reboot, Apple is finally ready to release its smart home hub. The tablet device has a unique interface that focuses on displaying data more than interacting with it.

Apple calls it HomeView. The name gets at exactly what its expected use case is — showing users relevant data and controls, all driven by Siri AI running on an A18 chip.

There isn't an App Store, but information and widgets can be donated by the user's devices. Users can also make FaceTime calls using the HomeView, get messages, or surf with Safari.

The HomeView will show static images, a clock, or other kinds of screensavers when not being interacted with.

"Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user," said Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. "It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it's powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone's information private and secure."

HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets, isolating private content. It's not clear if this relies on a shared home yet.

Homescreens aren't yet fully customizable. Instead, as rumored, they are Apple Watch-like, with complications and so forth.

Faces for HomeHub come pre-installed

The wall-mounted version can be attached using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. It's not clear yet if this is a standard VESA mount, or not. (Update: it's not)

Apple's wall-mounted HomeHub

Apple says that two custom full-range drivers in the display deliver room-filling Spatial Audio. A down-firing woofer and two force-cancelling passive radiators are built into the base. This makes it more like a HomePod mini, than the full-size HomePod.

The wall-mounted version also has two custom drivers and computational audio tuned specifically for on-wall placement. There is no woofer in that model, as there is no iMac G4-like base.

HomeView also works with a new lineup of smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. This, and compatibility is called the "Apple Home Collection."

In conjunction with those cameras and a iCloud+ subscription, HomeView provides end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, vehicles and more. With video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video footage, the device will summarize arrivals and so forth.

Customers in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the U.S. can pre-order Apple HomeView in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray for $299, today. Both the speaker base and a wall-mounted display cost the same.

But the mounts for the wall-mounted HomeView cost more. Those mounts will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. The Power Mount USBC Wall Connector is available starting at $59.95, with the Power Mount AC Wired starting at $79.95.

Shipments start on November 13.

items.title: The Apple TV 'hobby' has gotten far too expensive
items.content_html:
I've loved the Apple TV hardware since the first model. Unfortunately, I'm going to stick with what I have until I can't, because $299 for the box is just too much.

Ages ago, I got the G4 Mac mini because I was tired of burning DVDs and CDs. It was pretty nice to play media and games directly on my then-plasma Philips HD flatscreen.

Then Steve Jobs rolled out the Apple TV, calling it a "hobby" later in the year.

That "hobby" changed everything for me.

As the years went on, I got more and more Apple TV hardware. After a move about two years ago, I discovered seven Apple TV (third gen) and up models in my accumulated stuff, and four of the second generation flat black ones still around.

Some of this author's Apple TV 4K collection

And now, today, after 20 years of price cuts, with a period of time in there where the box sold for $79, we're back to $299 for the Apple TV hardware.

I understand that the RAMpocalypse is on us, the SSD media situation isn't a lot better, and it's only going to get worse. For now, from this chair, there is not enough difference in the hardware released four years ago to justify what is, in essence, a second price-hike in six months on Apple's lowest-end Apple Silicon it is presently shipping.

I'm not a fan of Google's or Amazon's streaming boxes. The performance is worse than the decade-old 1080p Apple TV with the App Store, and there are potential privacy issues.

Obviously, Apple's old streaming hardware hasn't been lit on fire with the release of the new one. I've seen the original Apple TV 4K for less than $100 on eBay. "Modern" Apple TV hardware with App Store support at 1080p is generally about $80 on eBay.

Don't get the older, thinner ones, though. Other than AirPlay, there's no future for those boxes at all.

There are more powerful alternatives for about the same price. Or you could AirPlay to your television if you can, and you trust what data it is collecting.

My suggestion, though, is to do what I did originally with that G4 Mac mini.

Find a Mac mini you like, and plug that into your TV instead. Hell, use an old MacBook Air, connect a USB-C to HDMI cable, and use it in clamshell mode.

If you shop smart, you can get a M1 Mac mini with 8GB of RAM and 256GB storage for about $380 on eBay. That's all you need to watch the Apple TV streaming service, get your Netflix on, or stream with Plex.

Headless M1 MacBook Airs go for about the same, and you get a keyboard for that. You can get really funky with that if you want, and get one of those HDMI wireless repeaters.

And if you do that, emulation is way easier than it is on the Apple TV hardware. For some reason, the Apple TV hardware is still very aggressive about purging storage, so emulation right now on it is pretty bad.

Sure. I will concede that you don't get the $1000-plus in new HomePods surround sound feature. That seems like a small sacrifice for more flexibility for the same price.

You do get Siri AI if you take this route, though. The Siri Remote works with the Mac over Bluetooth as-is. Adding a remote helper like Remote Buddy (paid) or SiriMote (free) will make that even better at a small cost.

I enjoy new Apple hardware for the most part. Spending $299 for an Apple TV box in 2026 is just not reasonable. We'll see what Black Friday brings, I guess.

items.title: HomeView's upcoming accessories let you build a smart home around one app
items.content_html:
As rumored, the new Apple Home Collection pairs LG and Schneider Electric hardware with home automation that keeps camera footage private, even from Apple. Unfortunately, nothing is shipping soon.

Apple HomeView is central to Apple's latest smart home push, with select Apple Home Collection devices available in December. Users can check cameras, unlock doors, and adjust the temperature without juggling separate apps or accounts.

The move shows Apple is poised to enter the smart home market, not as a device creator, but rather as a device manager. Partnerships with companies like LG would be mutually beneficial.

"Apple Home Collection makes it easy to choose smart home accessories with confidence," said Matthew Costello, Apple's vice president of Hardware Engineering.

"Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home, so managing your home is simple, reliable, and private."

Schneider Electric wall mounts are available when purchasing a wall-mounted Apple HomeView. Currently, customers have two choices: a $59.95 self-install USB-C wall connector or a $79.95 professional-install hardwire AC from Schneider Home.

Later, the options will expand to include a Power over Ethernet mount from Schneider Home for $129.95. Customers can also forego buying a wall mount, though Apple recommends against this.

Schneider Electric also offers two smart home accessories. These include a $199.95 Smart Home Thermostat and a $39.95 Home Room Sensor.

LG's Video Doorbell and LG's Smart Deadbolt Lock

LG's accessory lineup covers indoor and outdoor monitoring, a video doorbell, a smart lock, and temperature management. Beyond monitoring, compatible devices can coordinate temperature changes, lock doors, and activate cameras as household members leave or return.

Camera footage is processed on-device or through Private Cloud Compute, with supported iCloud+ plans storing 10 days of encrypted event history. According to Apple, camera footage and Home app data are never made available to LG, Schneider Electric, or Apple.

Eligible iCloud+ plans add Apple Intelligence video descriptions and natural-language searches, making HomeView more useful for checking what happened.

Apple says that availability will begin in December, with select accessories arriving in early 2027. Paid ADT installation will be available through Apple Retail for an additional charge.

items.title: New Apple TV 4K arrives four years after the last one
items.content_html:
The Apple TV 4K has finally been updated after a four-year wait, with the new model getting a new chip, microphones, and a new Siri Remote with Find My.

Updated as part of Apple's smart home-focused event, the new Apple TV set-top box looks a lot like the old one. Taking the form of the traditional spec-bump update, it looks visually identical to the previous model, with the main changes being internal.

Inside, the new model uses the A19 chip, up from the A15 Bionic introduced in October 2022. The change means better performance for apps and games installed on the Apple TV, with 50% CPU and 2 times faster GPU performance claimed over the previous model.

More importantly, it now supports Siri AI.

By supporting Siri AI, users can now ask questions that can take advantage of personal context understanding and a broader world knowledge, and conversationally, too. Users can ask things like "Where was Pluribus filmed?" or "Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?" with responses appearing a compact overlay.

Another change this time is an update to the Siri Remote, which now includes Find My support. This is something that should help users track down the controls whenever they lose them down the back of a sofa, especially when using Precision Finding.

An unexpectedly useful addition to the Apple TV is a set of far-field microphones echo cancellation, which can be used to summon Siri completely hands-free. This will be especially useful if users don't have a HomePod mini in the room, as it'll serve the same practical purpose but attached to a television.

While you can already pair HomePod with the Apple TV 4K, this has been upgraded too. Now, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience using the latest Apple TV 4K and four HomePod mini 2 speakers.

The HomePod minis can work together to determine their position in the room, calibrating audio timing and levels too.

While you do need the just-announced HomePod mini 2 for this application, you can also use the second-generation HomePod, so long as the front and rear speaker pairs match.

Sticking with device interconnectivity, the Apple TV 4K is still going to be a home hub for smart home devices. Even with the introduction of the HomeView.

There are other changes in the Apple TV too, such as how there's now only one version available.

Previously, you could get the Apple TV 4K in a Wi-Fi model with 64GB of memory or a Wi-Fi+Ethernet version with 128GB. Only the Wi-Fi+Ethernet remains, with the same capacity.

Wi-Fi has also been upgraded from Wi-Fi 6 to Wi-Fi 7, still with 2x2 MIMO, while Bluetooth has graduated from 5.0 to Bluetooth 6. Thread is still around, as is the infrared receiver.

The new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K can be preordered in the U.S. and 29 other countries now, priced at $299, with availability from November 13.

items.title: Europe's clashing with Apple means no HomeView for the EU
items.content_html:
Apple already denies European users Siri AI because of regulatory disputes, but now for the first time its hardware is being affected with no EU release for the HomeView.

The short version is that the European Union's Digital Markets Act (DMA) requires Apple to provide rivals with full access to its technology from day one. Apple argues that no other firm has this burden, and moreover that it dramatically compromises users' privacy.

This is why users in the EU have not had features ranging from iPhone Mirroring and Mac Live Activities, to Siri AI. And it's now why they will not get the new HomeView, at least not at first, and possibly not ever.

"Apple HomeView is not available for sale in the European Union, as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU," says Apple in a footnote. "Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward."

The word "constructively" is at best optimistic, though, as Apple and the EU have had heated clashes over the DMA. The EU's repeated position has been that Apple is wrong, that its demands do not affect user privacy at all.

But they do. Under the DMA, rival firms can request access not only to features such as the NFC technology behind Apple Pay, but also user data. And Apple reports that Facebook owner Meta has asked for far more access to private user data than any of its features or services actually require.

items.title: No biometrics are needed for HomeView to show a user's personal data
items.content_html:
Users of the HomeView will see a lot of personalized content on the display if it recognizes you. However, it will rely on your other Apple devices to do that.

The HomeView is billed as the center of a smart home, but it will also try to be at the heart of the lives of its users. As well as dealing with FaceTime calls and playing music, it will be providing access to personal content for each of its users.

The device is capable of recognizing up to six people, Apple claims, with each getting their own personalized Home Screen. While personal content stays private, shared items like photo albums and music can be used by anyone in the household and their guests.

The list of personalized content includes:

This is all serviced by Siri AI, which also means it can use a user's personal context. However, that requires you to pair it with a device that supports Apple Intelligence, such as an iPhone or iPad.

To make sure that only the right user sees their information, the HomeView can do facial recognition. However, it is not Face ID, as it's using the Center Stage camera without depth sensing.

According to Apple representatives talking to John Gruber of Daring Fireball, the camera is only part of the recognition system. Just as rumored, the system relies on other factors than just what the camera sees, or for voice, hears.

Apple presumes that the home that the HomeView will be used in is a reasonably safe space to begin with since it is used in the home. That is why Apple felt it could do authentication without on-device biometrics.

For users to be recognized by the system, Apple said they need to have a registered personal device nearby that supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. That device needs to be on the Wi-Fi network and have been recently unlocked.

That does rule out the Apple Watch from being used for recognition purposes since it can be authenticated similarly by an iPhone.

In effect, while the HomeView won't do any proper biometric checks itself, it will rely on you having authenticated properly on your personal devices instead.

items.title: HomeView doesn't play video apps natively, you still need an iPhone or iPad
items.content_html:
Apple has tried talking around the issue and even shown Apple TV screenshots, but now it's clear the new HomeView cannot play Apple TV or other video apps unless there's a CarPlay app for it.

HomeView looked at first to be great if you only wanted Apple's own apps, but now it seems you aren't even getting all of those. There are four Apple apps that have to be run on an iPhone instead:

It appears that the first three of those must be sent from the iPhone to the HomeView via AirPlay. It's not clear whether Apple News+ can be seen directly on the HomeView or will solely be read aloud by Siri AI.

So not only has Apple chosen not to allow any third-party apps at all, it's also limited itself. The lack of an App Store was already a bad decision, but now HomeView seems even more restricted.

Apple's description of the new device says very prominently that "Apple HomeView keeps you engaged and entertained with music, podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, and more."

But it obfuscates how two of those, audiobooks and TV, are not actually on the HomeView. Nor is the classical part of the Apple Music subscription.

Top: all of the native apps on the HomeView. Bottom: the significant ones that are not - image credit: Apple.

That's despite the HomeView details specifying that Apple Music and Apple News+ require subscriptions. The notes don't mention Apple TV at all.

Presumably there is a reason Apple couldn't include Apple TV, but it's hard to conceive what it could be. This isn't a safety issue as it might be with CarPlay, and even that now allows video apps when parked.

But yet, here we are. Apple is using CarPlay for the API for the HomeView.

It's not because of any deficiency in the HomeView's processor. True, HomeView has an A18 processor, which is older than the A19 in the newly updated Apple TV 4K.

Yet that A18 was used in the iPhone 16 range, and iPhones feature a native Apple TV app.

Rather than apps per se, the HomeView runs app widgets like CarPlay. The Apple TV widget on iPhone, for instance, simply opens the Apple TV app. Plus there is no Apple Music Classical widget on iPhone.

Whereas there is an overall Apple Music one and it includes a play button. So unlike many widgets, including Apple TV, it can play music without launching the app.

Apple Music therefore has what Apple calls an interactive widget. These were introduced with iOS 17 back in 2023.

However, this also points to how limited the functionality of the HomeView appears to be. It's already clear that it lacking an App Store of its own is an issue, but now even Apple's own apps are limited.

We'll see who adopts CarPlay functionality as time goes on.

Update October 13, 2:21 PM ET: The HomeView leverages CarPlay for streaming. If there's CarPlay functionality for media playback, it will work on the HomeView.

items.title: HomePod surround sound only available with new Apple TV 4K
items.content_html:
Four-HomePod surround sound has been rumored for a while, but the restrictions on what hardware is compatible is tighter than we wanted to see.

Apple is pretty clear about what's needed for that surround sound.

"Users can enjoy room-filling audio with a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or using multiroom audio. When paired with the new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2 supports four-speaker surround sound — Apple's most immersive home theater setup yet."

And in the footnotes of the PR for the new HomePod, it's even clearer.

"Home theater surround sound requires four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers in matching pairs (front and rear), paired with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) running the latest operating system software."

At least the full-sized second-generation HomePods can be included in the set. Although, including those as front speakers jacks a HomePod surround sound setup to $1000, not including the eye-watering $300 for the Apple TV hardware.

Going with four full-size HomePods jacks that up to $1400 for just the speakers. If you go this route, I hope ARC works well for you.

items.title: Beats x Pokemon collaboration reveal Beats Pill with Pikachu and Mimikyu art
items.content_html:
The latest Beats collaboration brings Pokemon to the Beats Pill, featuring everyone's favorite electric mouse and its ghostly doppelganger in special packaging launching October 15.

Beats by Dre is a subsidiary of Apple, who is no stranger to the Pokemon franchise. After a brief visit to his friend Tim Cook at Apple Park, Pikachu is now appearing on one of the company's products.

Beats and Pokemon have revealed the special-edition Beats Pill with Pikachu and Mimikyu art on the speaker grill. The gray speaker features Pikachu with electric bolts raised on the surface next to a grayscale rendition of the ghost Pokemon Mimikyu.

It's still the same Beats Pill you can buy in other colors for $149, but with a splash of Pokemon flair. The packaging is designed to let the Pokemon's ears pop up for display.

The Beats Pill packaging is custom and features Pikachu and Mimikyu

Also, a Beats By Dre first, the Beats Pill will include charms for the lanyard. They are a Pokeball, lightning bolt, and Beats "b" logo.

The speaker was revived in 2024 with improved audio, 24-hour battery life, and IP67 water and dust resistance. It works great with Android smartphones or iPhone, and supports Lossless audio when connected over USB-C.

Pikachu needs no introduction, as it is more recognizable globally than even Nintendo's Mario. The yellow electric mouse has been a staple of the franchise since its inception in 1996.

Mimikyu, however, is a more recent addition to the franchise. It is said to be a ghost Pokemon that built its costume from a rag to mimic Pikachu in the hopes that its popularity would let it make friends.

Peeking under that rag could prove fatal, as any that have seen what is underneath have died suddenly soon after.

The new Beats Pill will no doubt prove popular for Pokemon fans, and its arrival in October with Mimikyu front and center isn't a mistake. The spooky speaker will be available at Apple Stores and Target starting October 15 for the same $149 price.

items.title: Fourth betas of iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 land for testing
items.content_html:
Apple's now on the fourth round of developer betas for this generation, with new builds of iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, and macOS 27.2 out for testing.

The fourth developer betas for iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2 and visionOS 27.,2 have arrived, testing out more features before the update's eventual release to the public.

Typically, the first major post-milestone update is a point-one version, which isn't the case this time. As the iOS 27.1 build is designated to be used with the iPhone Duo, that version is being skipped for the non-foldable iPhone models.

The fourth 27.2 builds are:

New builds for tvOS 27.2 beta 4 and HomePod Software 27.2 Beta 4 have yet to arrive. This post will be updated if they do in the near future.

Apple has also released RC builds for other operating systems:

The fourth round follows after the third, which Apple shared on October 5. The second appeared on September 21, and the first round landed on September 16.

The first round introduced a few changes to iOS 27.2, including a redesigned Health app, which works alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Apple Watch Series 12.

FaceTime gained dual capture support, Siri AI added localization for multiple languages, and Apple TV profiles from tvOS 26.2 came over to the iPhone.

AppleInsider warns readers trying out beta software should do so on secondary, spare hardware instead of their mission-critical or daily driver devices. There is always a risk of buggy, broken, or other potentially harmful elements in beta software, which can be a risk to your data.

Members of the public should seek out the public betas instead of the developer versions as safer alternatives. In either case, it is also advisable to keep up-to-date backups on hand.
