items.title: Zimacube 2 review: A tinkerer's NAS, at a good price point
items.content_html:
The ZimaCube 2 is a six-bay NAS with no software lock-in. At $799, the Standard model suits tinkerers, though the company's Thunderbolt connection claims aren't accurate.

Once upon a time, I had a spare PowerMac 6500. Maybe it was a Performa — that specific is lost to me. This was just-pre MP3 explosion, but I still was generating a lot of data that I'd prefer not lurk constantly on my PowerBook 3400 first, then original PowerBook G3. What to do?

Then, in about the winter of 2002, hardware started aging less gracefully. The 6500 didn't boot one day, so the project to move the home server to a Beige G3 accelerated. Then a series of G4 towers, and more hard drives than was thermally wise in a 1,1 Mac Pro.

After the end of that, I shifted to external drive enclosures connected to a 2012 Mac mini, a 2018 Mac mini, and presently, a M1 Max Mac Studio.

Since about 2012, I've been reviewing network attached storage. Most have been appliances that you cram drives into, with a locked-down OS, and that's about it. Apple's AirPort and Time Capsule peripherals were like this from a file sharing point of view.

Some have been more tinker-oriented, some less. The ZimaCube 2 is on the more-tinkery side of that scale.

IceWhale takes a different view with the ZimaCube 2 that most vendors. Its ZimaCube 2 ships with ZimaOS Plus, but does not insist on it.

The hardware underneath is standard x86 architecture. Any compatible operating system will run, and that openness is the entire pitch.

The ZimaCube 2 uses a gunmetal chassis with a magnetic faceplate. It is meant to sit on a desk, not hide in a closet.

Six drive bays sit behind the front panel. A seventh bay handles SSD expansion.

ZimaCube 2 review: Bays at the front

The front also carries a USB-A port, a USB-C port, and an audio jack. The power button sits alongside them.

Around the back are the two Thunderbolt 4 ports and two 2.5GbE jacks. There is also HDMI 2.0, DisplayPort 1.4, a USB-A port, and the power input.

An RGB strip runs across the front. It breathes while working, and pulses red when a drive needs attention.

IceWhale claims noise stays around 30 decibels. We got a bit more than this with our Kanomax meter, but within the accuracy of the reader so we'll call this true. Drive chatter is most of the noise.

The enclosure feels very much like a sheetmetal PC case, and that's not a bad thing. There are no sharp edges, like some of the enclosures we've tested.

There are easily replaced and upgradeable fans, which is also a nice touch, considering they're pretty loud.

In a 36 dBi background noise office, idle the unit didn't add appreciably to that. Under load, both I/O and processing, the fan noise pushed that to about 42 dBi. When replaced by Noctua fans, that number went down to 38 dBi.

As I said, the standard model has six SATA bays for hard drives. Those take either 3.5-inch or 2.5-inch drives.

The seventh bay is a separate module holding four M.2 NVMe slots. That gives ten drive positions in total. These are bandwidth-constrained given the nature of the connection, so don't spend big money on PCI-E 5 drives here.

ZimaCube 2 review: Space for NVMe drives

IceWhale claims up to 212TB of capacity. That figure combines six 30TB drives with four 8TB NVMe SSDs.

The seventh bay is where the Standard model shows a limit. IceWhale rates its bandwidth at around 800 MB/s, shared across all four slots.

The Pro, at additional cost, and Creator Pack reach around 3,200 MB/s in that same bay. That is a four-fold gap for active editing work.

The intended setup is tiered. Fast SSDs hold active projects, while the hard drives handle the archive.

Practically, the SSD max speed saturates a gigabit network speed connection, and not much more. But, all six hard drives, properly RAIDed, can do that too.

Two Thunderbolt 4 ports sit on the back. IceWhale markets these as a 40Gbps direct link to a Mac, which isn't quite right. The ports use Thunderbolt Networking, not a direct storage connection.

Thunderbolt Networking sends ordinary network traffic over a Thunderbolt cable. macOS calls this Thunderbolt Bridge, and it sits in Network settings.

The practical difference is significant. The Mac mounts a network share, not a directly attached drive.

ZimaCube 2 review: Ports around the back

Real-world speed with that Thunderbolt Bridge tops out around 20 gigabits per second. That is half the 40Gbps headline figure.

IceWhale's own copy promises no network setup, which also isn't quite right. Thunderbolt Networking is network setup, just over a different cable.

It is still a genuine upgrade over the Ethernet ports, though. Two 2.5GbE jacks, even multiplexed with the right router, cannot approach 20 gigabits per second.

The marketing language oversells what is happening, and that's disappointing. This is a fast network link, not DAS-level direct storage.

The Standard model runs an Intel Core i3-1215U. It is a six-core, eight-thread mobile chip that boosts to 4.4GHz.

Two of those are performance cores. The other four are efficiency cores, an arrangement familiar from Apple Silicon.

Our test unit scores 1,771 in Geekbench 6 single-core. Multi-core came in at 8,083.

ZimaCube 2 review: Geekbench single-core results

Those numbers mean more in Apple terms. The 2020 M1 Mac mini averages 2,367 single-core and 8,445 multi-core.

So the ZimaCube 2 nearly matches that M1 Mac mini in multi-core. It sits about 4% behind, close enough to call even.

Single-core is a different story. The M1 leads by roughly a third, and single-core speed drives everyday responsiveness.

ZimaCube 2 review: Geekbench Multi-core results

The current M4 Mac mini stretches the gap much further. It averages 3,788 single-core and 14,727 multi-core.

That makes the M4 more than twice as fast in single-core. It is around 80% faster in multi-core.

None of this makes the i3 a poor NAS chip. Serving files and running most containers is not demanding work.

It does frame expectations, though. This is a competent home server processor, not a workstation.

Memory is the tighter constraint. The Standard ships with a single 8GB DDR5 module at 4,800 MT/s.

Two SODIMM slots sit under the lid, reachable after four screws. IceWhale rates the maximum at 64GB, using two spendy 32GB modules.

The single-module configuration carries a hidden cost. With one stick fitted, the memory runs in single-channel mode rather than dual.

Adding a second matching module improves memory bandwidth. For 8GB and Docker containers, that upgrade is worth budgeting for.

ZimaOS Plus ships preinstalled. IceWhale says the hardware runs other operating systems too.

The app store is where ZimaOS differs from its rivals. Every app in it is a Docker container.

Docker packages software together with everything it needs to run. Each app then sits in its own isolated container.

ZimaCube 2 review: Supplied in box

That means the catalog is effectively the whole Docker ecosystem. Hundreds of one-click apps are available, plus anything else containerized.

The trade-off is polish. These are community containers, not first-party apps built for the platform.

Synology offers fewer apps with tighter integration. ZimaOS trades that for breadth and freedom.

For anyone comfortable with containers, this is the appeal. For anyone who is not, it is a learning curve.

Two PCIe slots sit inside, one Gen4 and one Gen3. IceWhale pitches them as a blank canvas.

A graphics card fits, within limits. It must be low-profile and under 75W TDP.

That rules out most modern graphics cards. An external dock on those Thunderbolt ports is the alternative for anything larger.

Other options include network cards and SSD expansion. Few NAS boxes at this price offer that freedom.

The ZimaCube 2 Standard makes a clear pitch at $799. It is open hardware without software lock-in.

That openness is the real product. Anyone wanting to run their own operating system is well served.

ZimaCube 2 review: Cooling at the rear

The ZimaCube marketing oversells the capability of the Thunderbolt ports. Thunderbolt Networking is useful, and so is the possibility of adding a fast external enclosure or eGPU, but it is not direct-attached storage.

For Mac users, the Thunderbolt Bridge link is still worth having. It beats 2.5GbE comfortably for large file work.

On processing power, the i3 lands near a 2020 M1 Mac mini in multi-core. That is enough for personal cloud, backups, Docker, and self-hosting.

Anyone editing 4K daily should look at the Pro instead. Budgeting for a second memory stick is wise either way.

The ZimaCube 2 is pretty good. The operating system is mature enough. The hardware not fighting you if you want to install something else is the main selling point.

If you want Windows, install Windows. If you want TrueNAS, use that. No jumpers, no disassembly, and no nonsense.

The PCI-E card is a nice touch and is not common at the entry price.

Overall, the The ZimaCube 2 is a NAS that doesn't try to get in your way sometimes, like elephant-in-the-room Synology is doing more and more.

ZimaCube 2 is available from Zimaspace directly for $799. It is also available from Amazon for $769.40.

items.title: iPhone Duo production orders up 30% says report that does math strangely
items.content_html:
Yet another report from yet another source that has no real idea what Apple or its suppliers are doing, conflates parts orders with iPhone production. As before, this means nothing for iPhone demand.

As AppleInsider recently pointed out, and investment firm JP Morgan even more recently agreed, Apple has not cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro. Now a new report says that it must have cut those orders, because it's raised how many of the iPhone Duo it wants built.

According to Chinese financial news site STCN, Apple has increased orders for the iPhone Duo by 30%. This is for devices expected to be sold before the end of 2026.

The report seems to presume, for one thing, that manufacturing is a zero sum game for Apple. So if the iPhone Duo is up 30%, it says that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max orders are therefore reduced by up to 15% each, which is absolutely not the case.

But it also says that the new, higher order for the iPhone Duo does not exceed 10 million units. Rather than being an exclusive as claimed, that same figure was reported back in July.

Only, even if that means this new report has backing for its iPhone Duo figures, the percentages don't work.

Say iPhone Duo is now on exactly 10 million orders, and that it was therefore previously on around 7 million. This report claims that to make three million more of the iPhone Duo, Apple has cut three million iPhone 18 Pro orders.

But separately Apple is predicted to make around 80 million iPhones across the new Pro line and the iPhone Duo, in the last calendar quarter of 2026. Since Apple never releases figures, it's impossible to know, but it's easy to guess that a 30% drop in iPhone 18 Pro orders would be more than three million units.

Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Perhaps this is all because it's a confusing report in machine translation, but we've spoken to some more fluent folks than us, and they too think it's poorly sourced and written. It also appears to count the iPhone Duo as one of the Pro models, which is why it further calculates that the total amount of orders has not changed.

Then if the math wasn't enough, it appears that the entire report is based on components rather than finished iPhones. Apple has many manufacturing partners and uses many more component suppliers around the world.

As it has always been, component increases or decreases has very little to do with the number of iPhones produced.

So while it's possible that interest in the iPhone Duo has tempered that for the iPhone 18 Pro, none of this report is able to stand that up. And in the meantime, iPhone 18 Pro orders are such that shipping takes 10-12 days.

Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin on October 16. The device will ship, and be in stores, on October 23.

items.title: When Apple is shipping the rest of its 2026 hardware
items.content_html:
Apple has yet to ship a lot of stuff that's expected in 2026. From the certain date for the iPhone Duo, through the expected ones for the HomeView, and on to the probable MacBook Pro, here's when to expect stuff in stores.

Even before Apple formally announces its range of smart home devices, it has an unusual number of products expected to be released shortly. Here's what's coming plus when it is most likely to be announced and ship.

Apple added an extra date to its cycle of announcement, pre-order, and shipping, with a "Get Ready" option on October 12, 2026. But it's still the case that it is only starting on October 16 that you will be able to give Apple your money.

Apple's iPhone Duo, in action

Then on October 23, you will get your iPhone Duo. Or you will if you were fast enough and lucky enough. More than most iPhone launches, supply of the iPhone Duo is going to be extremely constrained.

It will be in stores starting on that same date, though. Maybe, depending on how many Apple made.

Reports claim that Apple's home hub, the HomeView, will ship in mid-November.

That's around a month after the announcement, so it's a shorter delay than the iPhone Duo had. It's conceivable that pre-orders will start on Friday, October 16, but Apple might want to keep that date clear for the iPhone Duo.

An example of what the HomeView could look like.

Pre-orders will surely start by at most a week before shipping, meaning it should be by early November.

It's possible that Apple's home releases will solely feature the new HomeView plus updates to the HomePod mini and the Apple TV 4K. But Apple is also preparing cameras and other devices in partnership with LG, which would benefit from being included in the launch.

The alleged Apple-LG smart home devices - Image credit: @pdfu/X

What's definitely coming at some point is Apple co-designed but LG-badged devices including a smart deadbolt lock. There will also be indoor and outdoor cameras, and a floodlight camera.

If those are announced at the October 13 event, pre-orders and shipping will not be far behind. It's anyone's guess, though, whether these devices will be immediately available, or slip into November.

That depends on whether they are ready in volume or not. And it might be useful to compare to the HomePod mini, which at least has an expected shipping date.

Apple's own smart camera isn't expected until 2027.

Unlike the HomeView and these cameras, there is already a HomePod mini on sale at Apple, but it's no longer the one you want. Instead, expect a new HomePod mini to ship on October 30.

An approximation of Apple's new pink and green HomePod mini speakers

It's most likely that pre-orders for the new HomePod mini will open on October 23. Note that at present, the Apple Store online is quoting a delivery date of between October 20 and October 27 for most current models.

Whether it will be called Apple TV 4K or will be renamed just "Apple TV" in order to further confuse people with the same name for the streaming service and the Apple apps, a new one is about to be announced.

The current Apple TV 4K.

Consequently there is again no official date, but reports say that the new Apple TV will ship on October 30. Pre-orders will presumably be on October 23.

In this case, the online Apple Store will offer some same-day delivery of the item. But in-store pickup will likely not be until November 4.

This is one of the furthest off of the expected new devices, but it's reportedly going to be announced on October 27. It should then ship by late October or at least before the end of November 2026.

Given the logistics of shipping all the other devices to stores, and making the maximum PR impact, shipping and even pre-orders are most likely to slip into November.

The current MacBook Pro.

When it comes, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro and 16-inch will feature a higher-quality OLED screen. It will also be a touchscreen, and Apple will see if there are enough fans of that in a laptop to make it a hit.

It will also reportedly be lighter than the current model. But the key selling points will be the touch-screen and the faster M6 processor.

Also rumored to be announced on October 27 is the next iPad mini. This is to have an OLED display for the first time, although it probably won't support the fast but battery-saving ProMotion of other iPads.

The current seventh-generation iPad mini sports an A17 Pro chip for Apple Intelligence. Credit: Apple

If correct, this will be the first update to the iPad mini since October 2024.

If the MacBook Pro is far off, an updated iMac is closest to a guess. By the end of October, it will have been two years since the iMac was updated.

The current 24-inch iMac

That was with the M4 processor, so there have been rumors that it will get an M5 upgrade, and perhaps the M6 like the Mac mini. If it does, it seems most likely to be announced alongside the MacBook Pro update believed to be on October 27.

This, too, would then mean it shipping some time in November.

After pre-orders and Apple's new "Get Ready" kind of pre-pre-order, eventually all of these devices will be available. It's still the case that only the base configurations will usually be available same-day, but this is when you will be able to buy without delay:

At least some of these dates will be confirmed by Apple during its forthcoming "Welcome Home" event.

items.title: Apple Maps Detailed City Experience comes to Austin, Texas ahead of F1 Grand Prix
items.content_html:
Apple's Pixar-like Maps upgrade has arrived in Austin, Texas to help F1 racegoers get around in style, plus Circuit of the Americas has some custom details in time for the Grand Prix.

Apple Maps has been updating F1 tracks around the world as races occur there. It is a part of promoting Apple's ownership of the US streaming rights of F1 using its various services.

The latest track to get special immersive details is the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Apple also took the time to update the rest of Austin with its Detailed City Experience.

Apple has been rolling out the Detailed City Experience to major locations in the United States since 2021. It's been a slow process, but has always been worth the wait when custom art and Pixar-like graphics are added to represent a city.

Visit the racetrack in Apple Maps and you'll see custom art for the track and various nearby attractions, like COTALAND Theme Park. The updated maps aren't just pretty to look at, Apple has worked to ensure information about grandstands, entry gates, rideshare locations, pedestrian walkways, and more are available in the app.

There is also a new Apple Maps Guide on country music singer Dylan Gossett's Austin Spots. Explore the highlighted businesses with their custom 3D artwork among highly detailed streets and foliage.

See Circuit of the Americas in detail ahead of the F1 Grand Prix

New 3D landmarks include the Apple Domain Northside, Black's Barbecue, LBJ Presidential Library, and the Paramount Theater. Notice small details, like birds flying over the Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge.

The F1 Grand Prix at Circuit of the Americas takes place on October 25 at 2:50 p.m. EST. It can be viewed in the Apple TV app.

items.title: There's a vibe-coded Adobe Creative Suite clone, and it's pretty good
items.content_html:
Vibe-coded alternatives to Adobe Creative Cloud apps such as Photoshop and Premiere have been released. They may help Mac users save money, but there are some nuances to the situation.

AI has been a major driver of change in the software development landscape, and it may have claimed its biggest scalp. A group of vibe coders has decided to take on Adobe by coming up with their own alternatives.

Released under the banner of ArtCraft, the releases on GitHub are referred to as "open-source, clean-room reimplementations" of well-known productivity software. Albeit software trying to be legally distinct enough from Adobe's products to avoid a lawsuit, while still being recognizable to users.

Said to be a combination of prompts to Claude Opus and developed in Rust, the initial releases include tools like Photoshop called PhotoCraft, Lightroom redone as LightCraft, and Premiere Pro as FilmCraft. Other Adobe products appearing in the repositories include Illustrator as VectorCraft, Acrobat as PDFCraft, and After Effects as EffectCraft.

They aren't stopping there. WordCraft is a take on Microsoft Word, alongside PowerPoint's DeckCraft, Excel's GridCraft, AutoCAD's CADCraft, and Avid Pro Tools' SoundCraft.

All of the cloned projects by ArtCraft are provided without any fees. Obviously, "free" Photoshop has helped the project get a lot of attention online, and they may stick around for quite a while.

That's assuming the Adobe lawyers don't try to pound them into the ground like a railroad spike.

The actual process of how the apps are being made are not fully spelled out by those behind the recreations. However, we can guess by claim of "clean-room implementations" that the apps were vibe-coded, rather than code being analyzed and copied.

While not a direct copy of Adobe's apps, it's safe to say that there has been a fair amount of inspiration taken from the interfaces.

Adobe Photoshop [left], PhotoCraft [right]

We downloaded PhotoCraft to see just how close the project got to the original. It turns out that it's very close, to the point that someone who knows Photoshop will potentially think it's a slightly different resolution to the one they're used to seeing.

Opening a blank document and pasting it in, there are obvious differences between the applications. For example, seeing colors and gradients by default isn't what I'm seeing in Photoshop, and there's no AI suggestions bar either.

But that said, there are a lot of elements that are almost identical. The left-hand tools bar, the icons on it, and the layers panel are very alike, if just tweaked enough to be a tiny bit different.

It's the uncanny valley, but for user interfaces.

We're very familiar with subscription services and the associated ire, especially when it comes to Adobe Creative Cloud's very high monthly fee.

However, the situation with what ArtCraft is doing is a difficult one to judge from a legal standpoint.

Assuming it's true, and we have no reason to to believe it isn't, the whole "clean-room" claim means that it's not a case of someone telling an AI to decompile code.

The classic example of that is Phoenix Technologies and American Megatrends making their own version of the IBM BIOS for PC clone manufacturers to use. That was found to be legal, after almost a decade of courtroom fights about it.

If the Adobe app clones were made legitimately without looking at the code, or decompiling the product being copied, then that becomes less of a legal issue.

What does remain a problem is recreating the overall interface. While there are typical conventions in play when it comes to user interfaces for specific kinds of apps, there is usually some level of variance between them.

Sure, you can rearrange the GIMP interface to be more like Photoshop's UI, but even that isn't directly copying every single element. The original GIMP layout is also a very different animal.

Here, copying the interface design is on purpose.

GridCraft [left], and VectorCraft [right]

The problem becomes one of finding where the line in the sand is. That, and working out what Adobe's well-funded legal team will be tempted to fight over.

As usual for a legal fight involving a major company, Adobe doesn't even have to win, but instead threaten others with expensive litigious action. That alone is a hefty threat.

While this may feel like a legal issue that can affect end users, it's tough to work out what could ultimately happen to them.

This isn't direct piracy of a product. You're not downloading Photoshop illegally, but someone's vibe-coded version of it.

But at the same time, since it is software that has been produced quickly using AI, it may not necessarily have the same style of battle-hardened code as the real thing. Indeed, the current iterations aren't at feature parity with the real things right now, and may never get there either.

The code is open-source though, and we know people are poring over it as we speak. From a security standpoint, so far, we haven't seen any untowards internet traffic to strange servers while using the apps.

What this does demonstrate is that anyone with enough money to pay for lots of Claude or ChatGPT tokens can quickly come up with full applications. Some that can look and act like apps made by a major corporation.

While this may seem like a potential lawsuit-based train wreck in the making, the next big attempt to take on Adobe could go a different route. One that stands up on its own, without leaning on Adobe's interface and feature set as a template.

That's what Adobe should be worried about.

items.title: How to set up your iPhone Duo pre-order to make checkout faster
items.content_html:
While pre-orders for the iPhone Duo don't start until October 16, Apple now allows you to prepare. You'll need to as demand is expected to be high.

It's usually the case that demand for a new iPhone is high enough that unless you're very fast, they go on backorder. You'll still get one, but it will be weeks later, sometimes months, so it helps to be as quick off the starting blocks as you can.

This time, though, the rush is real. Supplies of the iPhone Duo will be profoundly constrained.

The feature didn't roll out until 12:00 Eastern, but it's now live internationally too. So it is now possible to customize your iPhone Duo even before pre-orders officially open.

From October 12 through late on October 15, you can select your desired accessories, color, carrier, storage option, shipping address, billing address, AppleCare+ plan, and payment method. Some of this has been available since the iPhone Duo was unveiled, but now you can go through every step including any credit checks which normally delay orders, even momentarily.

This pre-pre-order process will shut down at some point on October 15, and then during early October 16, the Apple Store will go down. In theory it will reopen for the iPhone Duo pre-orders at 5:00 A.M. Pacific, 8:00 A.M. Eastern.

In practice, it will be a few minutes late and just how long it will take to reopen depends on a couple of factors. One is location, as this is a global release and different countries can have different waiting times, although you can expect the US to be the fastest.

Then there is also an issue of whether you are using the Apple Store online or on Apple's own store app. There it's never predictable which will open first, so savvy buyers use both.

Which does perhaps seem like overkill. It is unquestionably true, though, that at least most new iPhone configurations sell out incredibly quickly. In this case, with such a high-profile iPhone and apparently such supply constraints, shipping will surely slip back practically immediately.

This is an entirely new iPhone design, though, so perhaps more than usual, it might be wise to try one out in a store before buying. In that case, despite online supplies selling out, stores will have their own stock starting from October 23.
